findings.quote: Savings at risk of not being achieved in full this financial year (Amber): £0.750m (14.9% of target). The saving at risk of not being achieved relates to the switch off of residual street lights. Initial proposals have now been developed and are being reviewed.

findings.headline: Procurement savings of £0.774m rated at medium risk due to limited negotiating headroom
findings.detail: The council has budgeted £0.774m in procurement savings for 2025-26, but notes that the ability to achieve these savings is limited because current contracts and rates are already viewed as good or best value. There is little room left to negotiate further savings.
findings.matters: When councils have already extracted best value from procurement, further savings targets become increasingly difficult to meet and more likely to slip.
findings.figures: £0.774m (budgeted procurement savings)
findings.quote: The ability to negotiate or renegotiate rates / prices for on and off contract expenditure is limited as current contracts and rates are viewed as good or best. Risk that saving will not be achieved during the year.

findings.headline: Asset maintenance is being deferred, creating unplanned repair costs and insurance claims
findings.detail: This is a NEW risk identified in June 2025. The council is deprioritizing maintenance that does not meet essential spend criteria. This approach creates hidden costs: higher repair bills when failures occur, plus increased insurance claims.
findings.matters: Deferred maintenance is a classic sign of cash constraint. It trades immediate savings for larger unplanned costs and signals deteriorating asset condition.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: Higher repair costs to assets and/or moe insurance claims due to maintenaince not being undertaken that doesn't meet the essential spend criteria, which has a greater impact on budgets and is unplanned.

findings.headline: Circular Economy Act creates unfunded regulatory cost rising to £650k from 2026-27
findings.detail: The council has new statutory duties under the Circular Economy Act but has received no funding to implement them. Costs are minimal in 2025-26 but the register indicates ongoing costs could rise to approximately £650k from 2026-27. The council is awaiting further guidance from Scottish Government on implementation and whether additional funding will be provided.
findings.matters: This is an emerging unfunded statutory liability. If Scottish Government does not fund it, the council faces a £650k recurring cost from 2026-27 onwards.
findings.figures: £650k (estimated ongoing costs from 2026-27 onwards)
findings.quote: The Council now has new duties under this act which have not receive funding. Indications are that ongoing costs would be minimal in 2025/26 but could rise to around £650k from 2026/27.

findings.headline: Climate change impacts rated HIGH risk, with council already experiencing extreme conditions
findings.detail: The register explicitly flags climate change as HIGH risk. The UK experienced its warmest spring on record and driest in more than 50 years. Impacts include increased Bellwin triggers, unplanned reactive spend on weather events, and negative impacts on service delivery and landscape services.
findings.matters: Extreme weather is already happening (not a future scenario) and creates unbudgeted emergency spend that must be borne by reserves or emergency funding. The trend is expected to continue and worsen.
findings.figures: UK warmest spring on record, driest in 50+ years
findings.quote: UK warmest spring on record and driest in more than 50 years means that the risk around climate change remain high.

findings.headline: NESS electricity income could swing by £1m from grid outages outside council control
findings.detail: Electricity income from NESS (waste disposal facility) is highly uncertain due to volatile energy markets and SSE grid shutdowns. SSEN plans some outages this year but dates are unconfirmed. Grid outages could result in £1m loss of income.
findings.matters: This is a material income exposure (£1m) dependent on third-party infrastructure and global energy markets, neither of which the council controls.
findings.figures: £1m (potential income loss from grid outages)
findings.quote: A lot of uncertainty with NESS electricity income due to market prices and SSE shut downs which are outside of the Council's control. Grid outages could result in loss of income in the region of £1m

findings.headline: Transformation savings of £1.158m are flagged as high-risk and not yet secure
findings.detail: The council has budgeted £1.158m in transformation efficiency savings for 2025-26 on top of £1.436m carried forward from the prior year. The register explicitly notes the risk remains high and work is still underway to achieve the savings.
findings.matters: Lenders need assurance that budgeted savings are achievable. High-risk flagging on £1.158m means there is material unbudgeted pressure if these fail to land.
findings.figures: £1.158m (2025-26 transformation savings), £1.436m (carried forward from prior year)
findings.quote: Risk remains high - work is underway to achieve savings.

findings.headline: Winter maintenance budget has a £3m exposure between average and severe winters
findings.detail: The council budgets £8m for average winter maintenance, but severe winters could require £11m. The £3m gap between average and severe is not fully provisioned. Mild winters run ~£5m, creating a £3m variance across each category.
findings.matters: This is a known annual exposure where budget can swing significantly depending on weather, and the upper range is not funded.
findings.figures: £5m (mild), £8m (average/budgeted), £11m (severe), £3m gap between categories
findings.quote: A mild winter is estimated to be just over £5m, with an average around £8m (current budget provision) and a severe winter could be in the region of £11m. £3m risk between each category of winter.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Report to IJB 3 September 2025, 2025-26 Financial Update and Recovery Plan Update Appendix 2 Variance Explanations
findings.headline: Continence Service overspend £276k from increasing demand for continence products
findings.detail: The Continence Service (hosted by Aberdeenshire H&SCP) shows £276k forecast overspend driven by increasing demand for continence products with associated increasing costs.
findings.matters: Demographic service demand growing faster than budget baseline; signals trend in an aging population service area
findings.figures: £276,000 forecast overspend
findings.quote: The forecast overspend against the Continence Service is the result of increasing demand for continence products with associated increasing cost.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Report to IJB 3 September 2025, 2025-26 Financial Update and Recovery Plan Update Appendix 2 Variance Explanations
findings.headline: Community Hospitals £775k overspend driven by utility costs and high-cost packages
findings.detail: Combination of higher than budgeted utility costs and high-cost packages are main drivers behind £775k forecast overspend in Community Hospitals.
findings.matters: Inflationary pressure on utilities indicates non-controllable cost growth in health infrastructure; high-cost packages signal demand for expensive placements
findings.figures: £775,000 forecast overspend
findings.quote: A combination of higher than budgeted for utility costs and high cost packages are the drivers behind this forecast overspend.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Report to IJB 3 September 2025, 2025-26 Financial Update and Recovery Plan Update Appendix 2 Variance Explanations
findings.headline: Multiple services carrying staff vacancies that mask underlying cost pressures, forecast to persist
findings.detail: District Nursing (£335k underspend), Community Mental Health (£272k), Adult Residential Care (£300k), and other services show underspends primarily due to carrying vacancies assumed to persist through forecast. These represent deferred costs rather than permanent savings.
findings.matters: Apparent underspends are not structural savings but vacancy-dependent positions that will crystallize when positions are filled, creating hidden cost risk
findings.figures: District Nursing £335k underspend, Community Mental Health £272k, Residential Care £300k
findings.quote: The District Nursing Service has been carrying vacancies during the April to June period and it has been assumed for the purpose of the forecast that this be sustained.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Report to IJB 3 September 2025, 2025-26 Financial Update and Recovery Plan Update Appendix 2 Variance Explanations
findings.headline: Day care services £1m savings target at risk; £199k overspend due to voluntary severance and dilapidation costs
findings.detail: £1m saving was allocated to day care budget. Review of Day Services is in progress but currently showing £199k overspend due to potential voluntary severance and dilapidation costs not factored into initial savings targets. Forecast will be reviewed as work progresses.
findings.matters: Significant savings target undermined by transformation costs; pattern echoes residential care issue of savings assumptions not accounting for restructuring costs
findings.figures: £1m savings allocated, £199k overspend forecast
findings.quote: This budget had savings of £1million allocated to it. The review of Day Services is in progress. At this time the forecast is showing an over budget position of £199,000 due to potential voluntary severance and dilapidation costs which were not factored into the initial savings targets.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Report to IJB 3 September 2025, 2025-26 Financial Update and Recovery Plan Update Appendix 2 Variance Explanations
findings.headline: Primary Care Improvement Fund and Winter Pressure allocation funding not advised or received as at end May
findings.detail: Scottish Government Primary Care Improvement Fund allocation for 2025/26 had neither been advised nor received by end of May. Similarly, MDT allocation for 2025/26 had not been advised or received. Paper notes expectation that 2025/26 funding will be sufficient to meet costs, but timing remains uncertain.
findings.matters: Significant funding items unconfirmed mid-year creates cash flow timing risk and budget certainty uncertainty
findings.figures: Funding amounts not specified; funding expected to be sufficient
findings.quote: The Scottish Government Primary Care Improvement Fund allocation for 2025/26 had neither been advised nor received as at the end of May. The expectation is that 2025/26 funding will be sufficient to meet costs.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Report to IJB 3 September 2025, 2025-26 Financial Update and Recovery Plan Update Appendix 2 Variance Explanations
findings.headline: Learning disability care packages showing £468k pressure with packages still under practitioner review
findings.detail: Care First system indicating £468k pressure on care packages for adults with learning disabilities. Practitioners are still reviewing packages and this line flagged for continuous monitoring, suggesting further pressure possible.
findings.matters: Growing cost pressure in adult services with unclear resolution indicates demand-driven risk in high-cost care category
findings.figures: £468,000 pressure
findings.quote: Care First is indicating a pressure in the care packages for adults with learning disabilities of £468,000. Practitioners are still reviewing packages and this line will be continuously monitored.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Report to IJB 3 September 2025, 2025-26 Financial Update and Recovery Plan Update Appendix 2 Variance Explanations
findings.headline: Home care redesign stalled with £6.9m savings plan unclear; £5.22m overspend forecast and further redundancies flagged as possible
findings.detail: £6.9m in savings were allocated at budget setting for October 2025 implementation through service redesign. However, the anticipated redesign is no longer progressing as initially planned and extent is unclear. Voluntary redundancies agreed creating £300k in-year pressure, with service finance noting further redundancies may be necessary and continuing to clarify forecast position.
findings.matters: Large unachieved savings target with no clear delivery path and growing staff restructuring costs indicate service reform at risk and budget escalation risk
findings.figures: £6.9m savings allocated, £5.22m overspend forecast, £500k underspend due to current vacancies, £300k redundancy pressure identified
findings.quote: Savings of £6.9m were allocated at budget setting which were planned to take effect from October 2025. This service is undergoing a redesign but at this time it is unclear as to the full extent of the redesign. Some voluntary redundancies have been agreed which could result in a pressure of £300,000 in year and further redundancies may be necessary.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3 - Report to IJB 3 September 2025, 2025-26 Financial Update and Recovery Plan Update Appendix 2 Variance Explanations
findings.headline: Residential care £1.9m savings target abandoned; £2.499m overspend forecast as planned home closures shelved
findings.detail: Two care home closures planned during budget setting to deliver £1.9m savings were cancelled following officer appraisal. Officers recommended homes stay open due to high redundancy costs and lower-than-expected savings realisation, creating a £2.499m forecast overspend. Officers are now exploring alternative methods to achieve £800k of the original saving, with income also forecast £400k lower than budget.
findings.matters: Major failure of planned service transformation to deliver committed savings creates material budget pressure and questions delivery capability on planned reforms
findings.figures: £1.9m saving cancelled, £2.499m forecast overspend, £800k alternative saving target, £400k income shortfall
findings.quote: The forecast for this service indicates an over-budget position of £2.499 million. This situation arose because a £1.9 million saving was allocated to this budget line during the budget setting process, based on the planned closure of two care homes. However, following an appraisal by officers, it was recommended to the IJB that the homes remain open due to high redundancy costs and lower-than-expected savings.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Report to IJB 3 September 2025, 2025-26 Financial Update and Recovery Plan Update
findings.headline: Multiple operational budget lines are running over their forecasts: Allied Health Professionals, Community Hospitals, District Nursing, and Older People Residential Care.
findings.detail: Allied Health Professionals recruiting ahead of vacancy-factor assumptions; Community Hospitals over budget due to higher utility costs and expensive care packages; District Nursing experiencing higher vacancies than forecast; Older People Residential Care overspending on changes to how savings are delivered. These are pressures emerging in-year that weren't fully anticipated.
findings.matters: These operational overruns show that cost control is slipping across multiple service lines, not just in planned savings. This makes the full-year forecast even more uncertain.
findings.figures: NHSG Core Services forecast £1.806m over budget; Council Social Care £1.574m over budget
findings.quote: Community Hospitals is currently projected to exceed its budget, driven by higher than anticipated utility costs and the increased expense of high-cost care packages.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Report to IJB 3 September 2025, 2025-26 Financial Update and Recovery Plan Update
findings.headline: The 2026/27 budget cycle will begin with an underlying £17.155m overbudget position before accounting for inflationary pressures, pay awards, and demographic change.
findings.detail: The document explicitly states this position if no further savings are achieved in 2025/26. It notes that inflationary pressures, pay awards and demographic pressures are 'likely to add materially to the funding gap.' This signals a systemic inability to balance the budget without further council underwriting.
findings.matters: The IJB faces an escalating structural deficit. Lenders need to understand that Aberdeenshire Council is exposed to indefinite underwriting of a partnership with embedded cost pressures that current recovery plans cannot control.
findings.figures: Underlying 2026/27 gap: £17.155m minimum; actual gap expected to be higher
findings.quote: On that basis, the IJB will begin its 2026/27 budget setting process with an underlying overbudget position of at least £17.155m if no additional savings are identified in the current financial year. This position is before taking account of inflationary pressures, pay awards or increases to meet demographic change and assessed need, all of which are likely to add materially to the funding gap.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Report to IJB 3 September 2025, 2025-26 Financial Update and Recovery Plan Update
findings.headline: High-cost care packages are concentrating costs rapidly: packages over £1,200/week have grown from 11% to 16% of all packages but now represent 58% of annual costs.
findings.detail: Despite 587 fewer care packages overall, annual costs have risen £9.41m to £116.678m. High-cost packages (>£1,200/week) have increased from 452 to 507 packages and from £45.08m to £68.03m annually. This shift indicates demand is becoming more costly to serve, not cheaper, and undermines the Recovery Plan's demand-management assumptions.
findings.matters: If the service is delivering fewer packages but higher-cost ones, cost-control is failing. This is a structural driver of the underlying deficit and suggests savings targets based on lower costs-per-client are unrealistic.
findings.figures: Total packages: 3,172 (587 fewer since July). High-cost packages: 507 (16%, up from 452/11%). Annual cost: £68.03m (up from £45.08m)
findings.quote: Increased from 452 (11%) to 507 (16%), with an increase in annual cost from £45.08m (42%) to £68.03m (58%).

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Report to IJB 3 September 2025, 2025-26 Financial Update and Recovery Plan Update
findings.headline: The IJB's 2025/26 budget is only balanced because Aberdeenshire Council and NHS Grampian have injected £17.155m underwriting with no guarantee it will continue.
findings.detail: Both parent organisations are themselves facing significant financial pressures. The IJB has operated over budget for two consecutive years. There is explicit acknowledgement that this level of support may not be available in 2026/27, creating a structural £17.155m gap before inflation, pay awards, or demographic changes are accounted for.
findings.matters: A lender to Aberdeenshire needs to know that money it lends might be diverted to cover an uncontrolled health and social care partnership. The fact that this support is temporary and unsustainable raises questions about the council's underlying financial stability.
findings.figures: £17.155m underwriting commitment; starting position for 2026/27 budget: at least £17.155m overbudget
findings.quote: While Aberdeenshire and NHS Grampian have agreed to underwrite £17.155m in the current year, there is no assurance that this level of support will be available in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Report to IJB 3 September 2025, 2025-26 Financial Update and Recovery Plan Update
findings.headline: Agreed savings of £7.779m are now expected to deliver only £2.854m, leaving £4.925m unachieved.
findings.detail: The two largest savings projects have failed entirely: In-House Care at Home redesign (£3.107m planned, £0m achieved) and Establishment Review in-house care homes (£1.265m planned, £0.4m achieved). The remainder have been revised downward. This non-delivery is the primary driver of the projected £1.867m year-end overspend.
findings.matters: A lender needs the council's stated financial plan to be credible. When £4.925m of £7.779m planned savings evaporate mid-year, it signals either poor planning or unrealistic targets.
findings.figures: Planned: £7.779m | Expected: £2.854m | Not achievable: £4.925m
findings.quote: Of the agreed planned savings of £7.779m it is anticipated that only £2.854m will be achieved in the current financial year.

findings.headline: HRA New Build Programme temporarily paused pending outcome of HRA Business Plan review
findings.detail: As part of a review of the HRA Business Plan, the New Build Programme was temporarily paused to assess capacity across workstreams. This is a separate factor from external supply chain delays and suggests internal review of the HRA's financial capacity.
findings.matters: Pausing housing supply delivery raises questions about HRA financial sustainability and capacity, signalling potential stress in the HRA's position that warrants investigation
findings.figures: HRA capital budget £50.31m, actual £41.49m, underspend £8.82m
findings.quote: as a result of the review of the HRA Business Plan, the New Build Programme was temporarily paused to determine capacity across workstreams.

findings.headline: Capital expenditure came in £47m below budget—a 31% underspend—with major projects delayed by supply chain issues and contractor availability
findings.detail: General Fund capital spend was £60.60m against a £98.80m budget (38% underspend) and HRA capital was £41.49m against £50.31m budget (18% underspend). The total programme underspent by £47.02m. Major projects including Peterhead Community Campus & Levelling Up faced delays, and the Housing Improvement Plan slowed due to contractor labour constraints and material lead times.
findings.matters: A significant underspend indicates the council is struggling to deliver its capital programme on schedule, which raises questions about project delivery capability and may delay service improvements or economic impact
findings.figures: Total budget £149.11m, actual £102.09m, underspend £47.02m (31%); General Fund underspend £38.20m; HRA underspend £8.82m
findings.quote: Several programmes of works were delayed due to supply chain issues and revised start dates on major projects such as Peterhead Community Campus & Levelling Up. Other projects that faced delays were beyond the control of the Council, for example, the North East Integrated mortuary project.

findings.headline: HRA financing costs reached 19.97% of revenue, nearly 7 percentage points above the 13% budget
findings.detail: The HRA financing ratio significantly exceeded budget due to a shorter repayment period for loans fund advances and increased interest charges as the proportion of HRA debt outstanding increased. This represents a material variance in the cost of servicing HRA debt.
findings.matters: Unexpectedly high debt servicing costs in the HRA reduce financial headroom and signal pressure on the HRA's position, which is material to both the council's finances and potential lenders to the authority
findings.figures: 19.97% actual vs 13.00% budget; variance of 6.97 percentage points
findings.quote: Financing costs for HRA were higher than budget due to a combination of factors, including a shorter repayment period for loans fund advances compared to that originally budgeted and a variation in interest charges payable as the proportion of HRA debt outstanding increased.

news_drafts.headline: Staff capacity diverted to Museum of Aberdeenshire capital project is slowing resolution of audit findings
news_drafts.lead: Staff capacity constraints around a major capital project may indicate competing demand on management bandwidth, potentially affecting both project delivery and control framework oversight.

news_drafts.headline: 70% of loans out have expired agreements; 92% lack insurance documentation; 84% lack annual condition reports
news_drafts.lead: Uninsured loaned items and expired agreements create unmitigated financial and cultural loss risk; control failures mean items may be damaged, lost, or stolen with no recovery mechanism.

news_drafts.headline: Accreditation expires 31 August 2026 with re-submission due September 2026, while audit identified multiple gaps in required governance policies
news_drafts.lead: Loss of accreditation would damage council reputation, impact grant funding eligibility, and signal inability to meet professional standards; the tight timeline creates execution risk.
